solution: Total internal reflection requires two conditions at once. The light must pass from the denser medium to the rarer one (higher refractive index to lower), since only then does the refracted ray bend away from the normal and a critical angle exist; and the angle of incidence must be greater than that critical angle \(\theta_c\), where \(\sin\theta_c = \frac{\mu_2}{\mu_1}\). Going from rarer to denser, the ray bends toward the normal and can never be totally reflected, so the options in that direction are wrong. Saying "at any angle" is also wrong, because below the critical angle the light simply refracts out of the medium.

The particle starts from rest, so by the work-energy theorem \(\frac{1}{2}mv^2 = \frac{F_0 L}{2}\), giving \(v^2 = \frac{F_0 L}{m}\) and \(v = \sqrt{F_0 L/m}\). solution: Because the force depends on position, the work done must be found by integration: \[W = \int_0^L F_0\left(1 - \frac{x}{L}\right)dx = F_0\left[x - \frac{x^2}{2L}\right]_0^L = F_0\left(L - \frac{L}{2}\right) = \frac{F_0 L}{2}.\] The same result follows from the area under the force-displacement graph, a triangle of base \(L\) and height \(F_0\), whose area is \(\frac{1}{2}F_0L\). Since the particle starts from rest, the work-energy theorem gives \(\frac{1}{2}mv^2 - 0 = \frac{F_0L}{2}\), so \(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{F_0 L}{m}}\). Note that the force being zero at \(x = L\) does not mean the speed is zero there — the force was positive throughout the journey, so the particle has been speeding up the whole way.

value: \(\omega = \sqrt{4\pi G\rho / 3}\)
reasoning: At a distance \(r\) from the centre inside a uniform sphere, only the mass enclosed within radius \(r\) contributes (the shell theorem): \(M_r = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho\). The field is therefore \(g(r) = \frac{GM_r}{r^2} = \frac{4}{3}\pi G\rho r\), which is directly proportional to \(r\) and directed toward the centre. The equation of motion is \(m\ddot{r} = -\frac{4}{3}\pi G\rho m\, r\), i.e. \(\ddot{r} = -\omega^2 r\) with \(\omega^2 = \frac{4\pi G\rho}{3}\), so \(\omega = \sqrt{4\pi G\rho/3}\). Note that \(\omega\) depends only on the density, not on the radius \(R\) of the planet, which is why \(R\) appears in no option. Options C and D are non-physical: the motion is a genuine finite-period oscillation. Although the option text on this page is flagged as hard to read, option A matches the standard result exactly, so I see no reason to suspect a misprint.
solution: Inside a uniform sphere, only the mass contained within the particle's own radius attracts it — the shell outside exerts no net force. At distance \(r\) from the centre the enclosed mass is \(M_r = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3 \rho\), so the gravitational field there is \[g(r) = \frac{GM_r}{r^2} = \frac{4}{3}\pi G \rho r,\] which is proportional to \(r\) and always directed toward the centre. The equation of motion is therefore \(\ddot{r} = -\left(\frac{4}{3}\pi G\rho\right)r\), which is simple harmonic motion of the form \(\ddot{r} = -\omega^2 r\) with \[\omega = \sqrt{\frac{4\pi G \rho}{3}}.\] The angular frequency depends only on the density of the planet, not on its radius.
